newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers propose eliminating ethanol tax credits.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers propose eliminating ethanol tax credits.

text.p: Tax credits for ethanol put in place during the energy crisis of the 1970s to help lower U.S. dependency on foreign oil and improve the environment have not had that effect, a group of lawmakers said Thursday.

They released a report from the General Accounting Office (GAO) which said the tax credit had amounted to about $7.1 billion from 1979 to 1995, almost all of which would otherwise have been earmarked for the Highway Trust Fund.

"I have long considered the ethanol subsidy to be a wasteful use of tax dollars," said Representative Bill Archer, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee. "The subsidy has failed to achieve its desired environmental or energy-related intentions, while penalising taxpayers by removing money from our nation's road, bridges, and infrastructure," he said.
Legislation proposed by Representative Philip English, a Pennsylvania Republican, would terminate the tax subsidies after 1998. Similar legislation has not yet been offered by anyone in the Senate.

Archer, a Texas Republican, said the tax incentives would amount to $2.4 billion between 1997 and 2000. Ethanol federal tax incentives include a partial exemption from the federal motor fuel excise taxes that are earmarked for the Highway Trust Fund.
The GAO report said the tax credits had not lowered U.S. dependency on foreign oil nor would eliminating the incentives likely result in harm to the environment.

"Although available evidence suggests that the tax incentives for alcohol fuels increase ethanol fuel use, it also indicates that these incentives do not significantly reduce petroleum imports," the GAO said.
"Therefore, the tax incentives do not significantly contribute to U.S. energy independence," the report said.

Currently 95 percent of the U.S. production of ethanol fuel is derived from corn. Almost all of the alcohol used as transportation fuel in the United States in 1995 was either ethanol or alcohol used to make a fuel additive derived from methanol, GAO said.
The Renewable Fuels Association said the GAO report disregarded the benefits of ethanol production and use cited in the past.
